answer:
If you pay rent on the 6th, you will owe late charges under the lease. The lease states: “If rent is not received by 11:59 p.m. on the 4th day of the month, Tenant will pay an initial late charge of $75.00 and a daily late charge of $10.00 per day after that, but total late charges for one month will not be more than $175.00.” This clause is checked and therefore part of your lease (page 3, “4. LATE CHARGES”).

Rent is due on the 1st. The grace period runs through the 4th. Payment on the 6th means rent was not received by the deadline and remained unpaid for two days after the 4th (the 5th and the 6th). Thus, you owe the initial $75 plus $10 for each of those two days: $75 + ($10 × 2) = $95. The monthly cap of $175 does not apply because $95 is below that limit.

Florida Statutes chapter 83, part II (which governs security deposits, evictions, notices, etc.) does not regulate late charges; they are governed by your lease agreement. If the lease did not contain a late‑charge provision, Florida law would not automatically impose one.

**Answer:** You would owe $95 in late charges.

No further facts are needed to answer this hypothetical question.

answer:
No, your security deposit does not earn interest.

Under Florida law, a landlord may hold a security deposit in one of three ways: (1) a separate non‑interest‑bearing account, (2) a separate interest‑bearing account (in which case the tenant receives at least 75 % of the account’s annualized average interest rate or 5 % simple interest, whichever the landlord elects), or (3) a surety bond (with the landlord paying 5 % simple interest)【get_statute_section://83.49】(1)(a)–(c).  

Your lease states that the security deposit is held “in a separate non‑interest‑bearing account” (the box next to that option is checked)【THE LEASE: page 1, section 5】. Because the lease reflects the landlord’s choice under subsection (1)(a), no interest is required to be paid on the deposit.  

If the lease had instead indicated an interest‑bearing account or a surety bond, interest would be owed under subsection (1)(b) or (1)(c), but the lease you provided does not show either of those selections.  

Thus, based on the lease and the statute, your deposit does not earn interest.

Your lease explicitly states: “[X] This lease does not include an early termination option. If Tenant moves out early, Tenant is responsible for rent as Florida law provides.” (Lease, section 16).

If you move out before the lease ends, you may be responsible for rent as Florida law provides—typically, the landlord can seek rent until the unit is re‑rented or the lease term ends, minus any rent the landlord actually receives from a new tenant.
